mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide explicit equations or causal models beyond the description of the bound-token mechanism and Flow Matching loss.

experiments.title: Subjective Evaluation on WordVoice-5A Test Set
experiments.detail: Crowd-sourced listening tests with 20 participants rated 80 utterances per model on naturalness (N-MOS), speaker similarity (Spk-MOS), and word style control (Ctrl-MOS). WordVoice-Control achieved statistically significant improvements in controllability and naturalness over CosyVoice3.

experiments.title: Objective Acoustic Attribute Evaluation
experiments.detail: Metrics such as Word Error Rate (WER), Duration Mean Absolute Error (Dur-MAE), Energy MAE, Pitch MAE, Boundary Error Rate (Bnd-ER), and Tone Relative Error Rate (Ton-RER) were computed on Chinese and English test sets, showing WordVoice variants outperform baselines and ablations.

experiments.title: Temporal Control Precision Comparison
experiments.detail: WordVoice demonstrated lower Dur-MAE and Bnd-ER than MagicTTS variants on both Chinese and English test sets, confirming superior explicit temporal alignment.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies on Attribute Decoupling and Modulation Module
experiments.detail: Single-attribute control experiments confirmed decoupling of duration, boundary, energy, and pitch, with tone showing partial entanglement. Removing the modulation module degraded energy and pitch reconstruction, validating its role in acoustic detail compensation.

findings.title: Superior Multi-Dimensional Control
findings.detail: WordVoice achieves explicit, decoupled control over duration, boundary, energy, pitch, and tone at the word level, outperforming prior methods limited to unidimensional or implicit control.

findings.title: Improved Naturalness and Controllability
findings.detail: WordVoice-Control variant significantly improves naturalness (N-MOS) and word-level style control (Ctrl-MOS) over CosyVoice3, with p<0.05 and p<0.01 respectively, demonstrating effective prosodic planning.

findings.title: Tradeoff in Speaker Similarity
findings.detail: Localized prosodic variations introduced by WordVoice cause minor reductions in speaker similarity (Spk-MOS), reflecting a tradeoff between expressiveness and timbre consistency.

findings.title: Temporal Alignment Precision
findings.detail: WordVoice reduces duration MAE and boundary error rates compared to MagicTTS, confirming more precise explicit temporal control.

findings.title: Necessity of Acoustic Modulation Module
findings.detail: Ablations show that removing the WordVoice-FM module significantly degrades energy and pitch reconstruction, confirming its critical role in restoring acoustic details lost in token quantization.

contributions: Construction and open-sourcing of WordVoice-5A, a large-scale bilingual dataset with five-dimensional word-level acoustic annotations.
Introduction of the bound-token mechanism enabling explicit acoustic planning within an autoregressive LLM for multi-dimensional prosodic control.
Development of a fine-grained acoustic modulation module bridging discrete token representations and continuous waveform synthesis.
Comprehensive evaluation demonstrating superior word-level control, naturalness, and temporal alignment over state-of-the-art baselines.
limitations: Tone attribute control is only partially decoupled due to its dynamic variation nature, complicating absolute disentanglement from other acoustic features.
Strong localized prosodic manipulations slightly reduce speaker similarity, indicating a tradeoff between expressiveness and timbre consistency.
The approach relies on a large-scale annotated dataset, which may limit applicability in low-resource languages or domains without such data.
No explicit mechanistic or theoretical modeling beyond architectural design and loss functions is provided.
open_questions: How can tone control be further disentangled from other acoustic attributes to achieve fully independent manipulation?
Can the WordVoice framework be adapted or extended to low-resource languages lacking large-scale annotated datasets?
What are the impacts of explicit multi-dimensional control on downstream tasks such as emotion recognition or speaker adaptation?
How does the tradeoff between localized prosodic expressiveness and speaker similarity affect user acceptance in real-world applications?

papers.title: Estimating Uncertainty from Reasoning: A Large-Scale Study of Multi- and Crosslingual MCQA Performance in LLMs
papers.abstract: Uncertainty estimation (UE) enables LLM-powered systems to recognize when to abstain, yet existing research has predominantly focused on English. We present the first large-scale evaluation of UE methods across 22 languages, spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource settings. Using two human-curated Q\&A datasets, we compare open and closed box UE methods (nine in total) across different model sizes and architectures while eliciting long-form reasoning, avoiding LLM-as-a-judge and embedding-based scoring, which can introduce evaluation noise. We report three main actionable findings. First, we find that prompting models to reason in English while keeping questions in low-resource languages substantially improves UE performance, suggesting that comprehension of low-resource languages is largely intact, and that the reliability bottleneck lies in generation rather than understanding. Second, prompting models to reason in English closes the UE performance gap between low and high-resource languages, demonstrating that generation language matters more than the question language. Third, the choice of UE method should depend on model scale: at smaller scales, open-box probability-based methods outperform alternatives; at larger scales, closed-box self-verbalized uncertainty becomes superior. Finally, we provide an analysis of threshold selection for selective prediction, offering guidance on calibrating abstention in multilingual settings.

summary.takeaway: The study reveals that reasoning in English significantly enhances uncertainty estimation (UE) performance across multiple languages.
summary.problem: Existing research on uncertainty estimation has primarily focused on English, neglecting multilingual contexts.
summary.method: The authors evaluate nine UE methods across 22 languages using two human-curated Q&A datasets.
summary.evidence: Prompting models to reason in English while using low-resource languages improves UE performance, closing the gap between resource levels.
summary.limitations: The study is limited to two MCQA datasets, which may not fully capture the diversity of real-world NLP applications.
summary.why_for_you: This research is crucial for developing trustworthy LLMs capable of effective multilingual uncertainty estimation.

signals.text: Prompting models to reason in English while using low-resource languages significantly improves UE performance, indicating that comprehension is intact but generation is the bottleneck.
The study evaluates nine UE methods, including open-box methods like Token Entropy and closed-box methods like Self Verbalized uncertainty, across various model sizes.
The closed-box Self Verbalized method achieves an average AUROC of 0.72, outperforming other methods, particularly in high-resource languages.

deep_dive.overview: This research addresses the gap in uncertainty estimation (UE) methods for multilingual large language models (LLMs), focusing on the performance of nine UE methods across 22 languages. The study finds that reasoning in English while using low-resource languages enhances UE performance, suggesting that generation language is more critical than question language. The results indicate that the choice of UE method should be model-scale dependent, with open-box methods performing better at smaller scales and closed-box methods excelling at larger scales. This comprehensive evaluation provides actionable insights for improving multilingual LLM reliability.

methodology.title: Open-Box Methods
methodology.detail: These methods utilize internal model representations to derive uncertainty, including Token Entropy and Maximum-Sequence-Probability, which aggregate token-level logits into sequence-level scores.

methodology.title: Closed-Box Methods
methodology.detail: Closed-box techniques, such as Self Verbalized uncertainty, rely solely on generated text, prompting the model to express its confidence, although they may struggle with calibration.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: The study employs exact matching against human-curated labels for evaluation, avoiding automated ground truth matching to reduce noise and bias in UE performance assessment.

methodology.title: Data Sources
methodology.detail: Two human-curated Q&A datasets are used, covering high-, mid-, and low-resource languages, ensuring a diverse representation of linguistic contexts.

mechanism.title: Uncertainty Estimation Mechanism
mechanism.detail: The study does not provide a specific mechanism for how uncertainty is estimated but categorizes methods into open-box and closed-box approaches based on model access.

experiments.title: Evaluation of UE Methods
experiments.detail: Nine UE methods are evaluated across 22 languages using two models, Gemma327B and Qwen3-235B, with performance measured by AUROC.

experiments.title: Impact of Reasoning Language
experiments.detail: The experiments demonstrate that reasoning in English while using low-resource languages significantly improves UE performance, with the Self Verbalized method achieving an AUROC of 0.72.

experiments.title: Model Scaling Effects
experiments.detail: The study analyzes how UE performance varies with model scale, showing that open-box methods outperform at smaller scales while closed-box methods excel at larger scales.

findings.title: Improved UE with English Reasoning
findings.detail: Prompting models to reason in English while using low-resource languages improves UE performance, indicating a generation bottleneck.

findings.title: Language Generation Matters
findings.detail: The performance gap in UE between low and high-resource languages is closed when models reason in English, highlighting the importance of generation language.

findings.title: Model Scale Dependency
findings.detail: At smaller model scales, open-box methods like Token Entropy outperform closed-box methods, while at larger scales, closed-box methods like Self Verbalized uncertainty become superior.

contributions: First large-scale evaluation of UE methods across 22 languages.
Identification of the importance of reasoning language over question language in UE performance.
Guidance on selecting UE methods based on model scale.
limitations: Focus on only two MCQA datasets may not represent the full diversity of NLP applications.
Exclusion of training-based UE methods limits the scope of the analysis.
open_questions: How can UE methods be further improved for low-resource languages?
What are the implications of different UE methods in real-world applications?

papers.title: From Voting to Agent Collaboration: Answer-Type-Aware LLM Pipelines for BioASQ 14b
papers.abstract: Biomedical question answering requires not only accurate extraction of information from scientific literature but also reliable integration of evidence across multiple documents. This study presents a question-type-specific large language model (LLM) framework for BioASQ 14b Task B, designed to improve answer robustness and evidence grounding in biomedical question answering. Rather than applying a single prompting strategy to all questions, the framework selects different inference procedures for yes/no, factoid, and list questions according to their distinct reasoning and evaluation requirements. For yes/no questions, snippet shuffling and self-reflection are used to reduce sensitivity to evidence ordering and improve decision stability. For factoid questions, full-snippet input is combined with chain-of-thought-based in-context learning to support accurate biomedical entity identification. For list questions, a multi-agent architecture is employed, in which evidence extraction, candidate generation, answer verification, and final aggregation are handled collaboratively. Preliminary experiments on BioASQ 13b were used to identify effective inference strategies for each question type, and the resulting framework was subsequently evaluated in the official BioASQ 14b Task B challenge. In the official evaluation, our framework showed competitive performance across multiple batches and achieved first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining question-type-specific inference, ensemble prediction, and agent-based verification for reliable biomedical question answering.

summary.takeaway: The proposed LLM framework enhances biomedical question answering by tailoring inference strategies to specific question types.
summary.problem: Biomedical question answering faces challenges in accurately integrating evidence from diverse sources.
summary.method: The framework employs question-type-specific inference procedures, including snippet shuffling and multi-agent collaboration.
summary.evidence: In the BioASQ 14b Task B challenge, the framework achieved first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4, demonstrating its effectiveness.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide detailed performance metrics for all question types across all batches.
summary.why_for_you: This research offers insights into improving LLM performance in specialized domains, relevant for trustworthy AI applications.

signals.text: The framework achieved a macro F1 score of 0.9110 for yes/no questions, indicating strong decision-making capabilities.
Utilizing a multi-agent architecture for list questions allows for collaborative evidence extraction and verification, enhancing answer reliability.
The use of snippet shuffling in yes/no questions reduced sensitivity to evidence ordering, improving decision stability and consistency.

deep_dive.overview: This research addresses the complexities of biomedical question answering by introducing a question-type-specific LLM framework for the BioASQ 14b Task B challenge. The framework adapts inference strategies for yes/no, factoid, and list questions, enhancing answer robustness and evidence grounding. Preliminary experiments on BioASQ 13b informed the selection of effective strategies, leading to competitive performance in the official evaluation, particularly achieving first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4. This demonstrates the potential of tailored inference methods in improving LLM capabilities in biomedical contexts.

methodology.title: Yes/No Question Processing
methodology.detail: The yes/no subsystem employs snippet shuffling and self-reflection to enhance decision stability. It utilizes an ensemble of four LLM configurations, querying each with varied snippet orders and aggregating results through majority voting.

methodology.title: Factoid Question Processing
methodology.detail: For factoid questions, the framework combines full-snippet input with chain-of-thought-based in-context learning to accurately identify biomedical entities, ensuring precise responses.

methodology.title: List Question Processing
methodology.detail: A multi-agent architecture is implemented for list questions, where evidence extraction, candidate generation, and answer verification are conducted collaboratively, improving overall answer quality.

mechanism.title: Ensemble Voting Mechanism
mechanism.detail: The yes/no subsystem utilizes a majority voting mechanism among multiple LLM outputs, with a verification agent employed when outputs conflict, ensuring robust decision-making.

experiments.title: BioASQ 13b Development Benchmark
experiments.detail: Preliminary experiments on the BioASQ 13b test set were conducted to evaluate various prompting strategies and model configurations, informing the final system design for BioASQ 14b.

experiments.title: Official BioASQ 14b Evaluation
experiments.detail: The framework was evaluated across four batches in the BioASQ 14b challenge, achieving an average score of 0.9110 for yes/no macro F1 and first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4.

findings.title: Performance in Yes/No Questions
findings.detail: The framework achieved a macro F1 score of 0.9110 for yes/no questions, indicating effective handling of binary decisions.

findings.title: Factoid Question Success
findings.detail: The system ranked first in the factoid subtask of Batch 4, demonstrating superior performance in identifying specific biomedical entities.

findings.title: List Question Challenges
findings.detail: The multi-agent architecture for list questions improved evidence integration, although specific performance metrics for this category were not detailed.

contributions: Introduction of a question-type-specific LLM framework for biomedical question answering.
Demonstration of effective ensemble strategies for improving answer robustness.
Implementation of a multi-agent architecture for collaborative evidence processing.
limitations: Lack of detailed performance metrics for list questions across all batches.
No comprehensive analysis of the impact of individual LLM configurations on overall performance.
open_questions: How can the framework be adapted for other domains beyond biomedical question answering?
What are the implications of varying LLM configurations on performance across different question types?

papers.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Direct On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a powerful recipe for improving language-model reasoning, but it is expensive to repeat on every new strong model because the target model must generate many rollouts during training. As models scale, post-training itself becomes a bottleneck. We study a weak-to-strong alternative: run RL on a smaller model where rollouts are cheaper, then reuse what that RL run learned to improve a stronger target model. Directly distilling the post-RL weak teacher is not enough, because the teacher's final policy mixes useful RL gains with the limitations of the smaller model. We propose Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD), which transfers the teacher's RL-induced policy shift instead. Direct-OPD compares the post-RL teacher with its own pre-RL reference and treats their log-ratio as a dense implicit reward for the student. In plain terms, the checkpoint pair tells us which actions RL made the weak model more or less likely to take, and Direct-OPD applies that signal on the stronger student's own on-policy states. This directly reuses the weak model's RL supervision signal without training an explicit reward model or running sparse-reward RL on the target model. Empirically, Direct-OPD consistently leverages weaker teachers to improve stronger target models; notably, it boosts Qwen3-1.7B from 48.3% to 62.4% on AIME 2024 in just 4 hours on 8 A100 GPUs. It outperforms step-matched direct RL and enables the sequential composition of multiple policy shifts. Our results show that RL outcomes can be reused across model scales as implicit reward signals, not merely as final models to imitate.

summary.takeaway: Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD) effectively enhances stronger language models by leveraging the policy shifts from weaker models trained with reinforcement learning.
summary.problem: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is computationally expensive for large models, creating a bottleneck in post-training.
summary.method: Direct-OPD transfers the RL-induced policy shift from a weaker model to a stronger model, treating the log-ratio of their policies as an implicit reward.
summary.evidence: Direct-OPD improved the Qwen3-1.7B model's performance from 48.3% to 62.4% on AIME 2024 in just 4 hours using 8 A100 GPUs.
summary.limitations: The effectiveness of Direct-OPD is conditional on the meaningfulness of the teacher/reference improvement on student-visited states.
summary.why_for_you: This research provides insights into efficient model training strategies, relevant for those focused on on-policy distillation and statistical theory for LLMs.

signals.text: Direct-OPD enables the transfer of RL-induced policy shifts rather than the final policy of the teacher, allowing stronger models to benefit from weaker ones without direct imitation.
The method utilizes the log-ratio of the post-RL teacher's policy against its pre-RL reference as a dense implicit reward, circumventing the need for an explicit reward model.
Empirical results demonstrate that Direct-OPD consistently improves stronger models across various teacher pairs and student families, indicating its robustness and generalizability.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of costly reinforcement learning (RL) processes in training large language models by proposing Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD). This method allows for the efficient transfer of RL-induced policy shifts from a weaker model to a stronger one, effectively reusing the RL supervision signal without the need for extensive rollouts on the target model. The strongest evidence supporting this approach is the significant performance boost of the Qwen3-1.7B model, which increased from 48.3% to 62.4% accuracy on AIME 2024 in a short training period, showcasing the potential of Direct-OPD in enhancing model capabilities while reducing computational costs.

methodology.title: Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD)
methodology.detail: Direct-OPD involves running RL on a smaller, cheaper model and transferring the learned policy shift to a stronger model. The method compares the post-RL teacher's policy with its pre-RL reference, using their log-ratio as an implicit reward for the student.

methodology.title: Policy Shift Transfer
methodology.detail: The transfer process focuses on the behavioral changes induced by the RL training of the weak model, rather than attempting to replicate the weak model's final policy, ensuring that stronger models can leverage useful RL insights.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: The evaluation of model performance is conducted using the AIME benchmarks, with specific metrics such as accuracy averaged over multiple samples to assess the effectiveness of the Direct-OPD approach.

mechanism.title: Policy-as-Reward Identity
mechanism.detail: Direct-OPD leverages the policy-as-reward identity, where the log-ratio of policies under KL-regularized RL can recover the reward signal, allowing for effective transfer of learned behaviors.

experiments.title: Improvement of Stronger Students
experiments.detail: In experiments, the policy shift from R1-Distill-1.5B to JustRL-1.5B was transferred to stronger models like R1-Distill-7B and Qwen3-4B, showing consistent performance improvements across different model families.

experiments.title: Comparison with Direct RL
experiments.detail: Direct-OPD was compared against step-matched direct RL, demonstrating superior performance in both accuracy and computational efficiency, validating the effectiveness of the proposed method.

experiments.title: Sequential Composition of Policy Shifts
experiments.detail: The ability to compose multiple independently learned policy shifts was tested, confirming that Direct-OPD can accumulate gains in a single student model, enhancing its overall performance.

findings.title: Effective Transfer Across Models
findings.detail: Direct-OPD successfully improved the performance of stronger models, such as Qwen3-1.7B, by utilizing policy shifts from weaker models, demonstrating the method's versatility.

findings.title: Significant Performance Gains
findings.detail: The Qwen3-1.7B model achieved a notable accuracy increase from 48.3% to 62.4% on AIME 2024, showcasing the practical benefits of Direct-OPD.

findings.title: Generalizability of Direct-OPD
findings.detail: The method proved effective across various teacher pairs and student families, indicating that Direct-OPD is not limited to specific model architectures or training data.

contributions: Introduction of Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD) as a novel approach for weak-to-strong model training.
Demonstration of the effectiveness of transferring RL-induced policy shifts rather than final policies.
Empirical validation of Direct-OPD's performance improvements across different model families and training setups.
limitations: The signal's effectiveness is conditional on the meaningfulness of the teacher/reference improvement on student-visited states.
The best response length and KL strength remain dependent on the specific teacher-student pair.
open_questions: How can the conditional nature of the signal be mitigated to ensure consistent performance across all model pairs?
What are the optimal configurations for KL strength and response length in various training scenarios?

papers.title: Clinician-Level Agreement Without Clinical Caution: LLM Evaluator Limits in Medical AI Benchmarking
papers.abstract: Open-response evaluation provides stronger clinical validity than multiple-choice benchmarks but creates a scoring bottleneck that motivates automated LLM-asa-Judge approaches. Whether such evaluators replicate clinical calibration and caution, however, remains untested. We introduce MedQADE, the first standardised open-response clinical benchmark for German, a major clinical language lacking native evaluation infrastructure, comprising 3,800 items annotated by ten practising physicians and nine Large Language Model (LLM) evaluators. The top-performing evaluator model, Gemini 3 Flash, reached alignment consistent with the physician ceiling (\k{appa} = 0.694 vs. \k{appa} = 0.709), though wide confidence intervals limit interpretation. Despite this statistical alignment, automated evaluators exhibited near-absent clinical metacognition: physicians scaled abstention with item difficulty, while frontier models assigned definitive scores in every case. We additionally quantified systematic lineage-dependent biases, where models preferentially scored architectural siblings, an effect independent of language. These results show that statistical alignment does not ensure clinical caution, and that evaluator independence requires explicit verification.

summary.takeaway: Automated LLM evaluators can statistically align with physician judgments on open-response clinical benchmarks but fail to exhibit clinical caution and metacognition.
summary.problem: Current medical LLM evaluation relies heavily on multiple-choice benchmarks that inadequately capture clinical reasoning and lack native evaluation resources for languages like German.
summary.method: The study introduces MedQADE, a standardized German open-response clinical benchmark with 3,800 items annotated by physicians and nine LLM evaluators, comparing their agreement and clinical metacognition.
summary.evidence: Gemini 3 Flash achieved a kappa agreement of 0.694 close to the physician ceiling of 0.709, yet LLM evaluators assigned definitive scores without abstention, unlike physicians who scaled abstention by item difficulty.
summary.limitations: Wide confidence intervals in agreement metrics limit interpretation, and the study identifies systematic lineage-dependent biases in LLM evaluators that require further investigation.
summary.why_for_you: This work highlights critical gaps in trusting LLM evaluators for clinical AI benchmarking, emphasizing the need to verify evaluator independence and clinical caution beyond statistical alignment.

signals.text: Gemini 3 Flash, the top-performing LLM evaluator, reached a kappa agreement of 0.694 with physician annotations on MedQADE, nearly matching the physician inter-rater ceiling of 0.709, demonstrating strong statistical alignment.

MedQADE was constructed from the Ankizin flashcard corpus, filtered to 26,598 single-cloze clinical questions, and annotated by ten practicing physicians and nine LLM evaluators, enabling open-response evaluation in German clinical NLP.

Despite statistical agreement, LLM evaluators showed near-absent clinical metacognition by assigning definitive scores to all items, whereas physicians abstained more frequently on difficult items, indicating a lack of clinical caution in automated judgments.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the inadequacy of multiple-choice benchmarks in evaluating clinical reasoning of LLMs, especially in German where native resources are scarce. It introduces MedQADE, a large-scale open-response clinical benchmark derived from a peer-reviewed German medical flashcard corpus. The study compares annotations from ten physicians and nine LLM evaluators, including Gemini 3 Flash, across 3,800 items. While Gemini 3 Flash achieved near-physician-level statistical agreement (kappa 0.694 vs. 0.709), the LLMs failed to replicate clinical metacognition, as they never abstained from scoring regardless of item difficulty. Additionally, the study reveals lineage-dependent biases where LLM evaluators favor architectural siblings, independent of language. These findings demonstrate that statistical alignment alone is insufficient to ensure clinical caution or evaluator independence, underscoring the need for explicit verification of automated evaluators in medical AI benchmarking.

methodology.title: Dataset Formulation and Processing
methodology.detail: MedQADE was created from the Ankizin project’s version 5 flashcard collection, a German medical study tool with peer-reviewed clinical validity. The dataset was filtered to 26,598 single-cloze deletion items to ensure open-response format, suitable for evaluating free recall clinical knowledge.

methodology.title: LLM Student Generation
methodology.detail: Five LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5 Nano, Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 3 4B, Qwen3-4B) generated synthetic answers for all single-cloze items using a German-language system prompt simulating a high-stakes medical exam. Generation temperature was fixed at 0.2 to balance precision and variability.

methodology.title: Annotation Design and Evaluation
methodology.detail: Ten practicing physicians and nine LLM evaluators independently scored 3,800 MedQADE items. Agreement was measured using Krippendorff’s alpha and Cohen’s kappa. Abstention behavior and scoring biases were analyzed to assess clinical metacognition and evaluator independence.

mechanism.title: Clinical Metacognition Mechanism
mechanism.detail: No explicit mechanistic model is provided; however, the study operationalizes clinical metacognition as the ability to abstain from scoring on difficult items, a behavior observed in physicians but absent in LLM evaluators, indicating a qualitative difference in judgment calibration.

experiments.title: Evaluator Agreement Experiment
experiments.detail: Nine LLM evaluators and ten physicians scored 3,800 MedQADE items. Agreement metrics (kappa) were computed, showing Gemini 3 Flash achieved 0.694, close to the physician ceiling of 0.709, with wide confidence intervals noted.

experiments.title: Abstention Behavior Analysis
experiments.detail: Physician annotators scaled abstention rates with item difficulty, whereas LLM evaluators assigned definitive scores to all items, revealing a lack of clinical caution in automated evaluation.

experiments.title: Lineage-Dependent Bias Quantification
experiments.detail: The study identified systematic biases where LLM evaluators preferentially scored outputs from architectural siblings, independent of language, suggesting evaluator dependence on model lineage.

findings.title: Statistical Agreement
findings.detail: Gemini 3 Flash’s kappa agreement of 0.694 closely matches the physician inter-rater ceiling of 0.709, indicating strong statistical alignment between automated and human evaluators.

findings.title: Absence of Clinical Metacognition
findings.detail: Unlike physicians who abstained more on difficult items, LLM evaluators assigned definitive scores in every case, demonstrating near-absent clinical metacognition.

findings.title: Lineage-Dependent Bias
findings.detail: LLM evaluators showed systematic preference for scoring architectural sibling models, an effect independent of language, indicating evaluator bias linked to model lineage.

contributions: Introduction of MedQADE, the first standardized open-response clinical benchmark for German with expert physician and LLM annotations.
Demonstration that statistical agreement metrics alone do not capture clinical caution or metacognition in LLM evaluators.
Identification of lineage-dependent biases in LLM evaluators, highlighting the need for explicit verification of evaluator independence.
Provision of a methodology combining open-response clinical questions with multi-annotator evaluation to better assess LLM clinical reasoning.
limitations: Wide confidence intervals in kappa agreement metrics limit the robustness of statistical alignment claims.
Absence of mechanistic modeling for clinical metacognition restricts understanding of underlying evaluator behaviors.
Potential bias introduced by using synthetic LLM-generated student answers was not fully explored.
The study focuses on German clinical language, limiting immediate generalizability to other languages or clinical contexts.
open_questions: How can clinical metacognition be explicitly modeled and integrated into LLM evaluators to improve clinical caution?
What methods can mitigate lineage-dependent biases in automated LLM evaluation to ensure evaluator independence?
Can open-response benchmarks like MedQADE be extended or adapted to other languages and clinical domains effectively?
How do synthetic LLM-generated student answers impact the evaluation of LLM evaluators compared to real human responses?

papers.title: Antaeus: Hunting Repository-Level Logic Vulnerabilities via Context-Grounded LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: LLM-based vulnerability detectors have shown promising results in identifying memory-safety bugs and vulnerability classes whose violations can often be expressed through established security properties. Logic vulnerabilities, however, pose a different challenge, as their identification requires inferring application-specific security invariants and implicit assumptions about intended behavior. Even frontier agentic models struggle because these invariants are often implicit and buried among unrelated code. Motivated by this gap, we present Antaeus, a framework for detecting logic vulnerabilities that grounds LLM reasoning in repository-level code context. Antaeus follows a repository-scale pipeline combining function prioritization, context-grounded reasoning, comparative validation, and structured reporting. It ranks functions using lightweight repo-wide security signals, directing costly LLM analysis toward relevant code and reducing calls, cost, and triage effort. For each prioritized function, Antaeus combines local code context with a repository-level view of the application's functionality, security resources, and trust boundaries. This enables reasoning about how the function is executed within the broader application rather than as an isolated snippet. Antaeus identifies security-sensitive sinks, derives safety conditions for safe execution, and checks whether they are locally satisfied. Candidate findings undergo comparative validation, pruning concerns that reflect project-wide norms rather than distinctive violations. Finally, Antaeus reports sinks, violated safety conditions, and evidence, making findings actionable and traceable. We evaluate Antaeus on 28 repositories with confirmed logic vulnerabilities and compare it against function-level and agentic models. Antaeus detects and explains 15 vulnerabilities, outperforming baselines with comparable token usage and cost.

summary.takeaway: Antaeus effectively detects repository-level logic vulnerabilities by grounding LLM reasoning in prioritized, context-rich code views, outperforming function-level and agentic baselines with comparable cost.
summary.problem: Logic vulnerabilities require inferring implicit, application-specific security invariants distributed across large codebases, which frontier LLMs struggle to identify from isolated code snippets or exhaustive search.
summary.method: Antaeus combines lightweight function prioritization, context-grounded LLM reasoning incorporating repository-level evidence, comparative validation to prune false positives, and structured reporting of sinks and violated safety conditions.
summary.evidence: Evaluation on 28 real-world repositories with confirmed logic vulnerabilities shows Antaeus detects and explains 15 vulnerabilities, substantially outperforming function-level and agentic baselines while maintaining similar token usage and cost.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed quantitative analysis of false positive rates or scalability beyond the 28 evaluated repositories, and the approach depends on heuristic prioritization and domain-specific sink and safety condition definitions.
summary.why_for_you: Antaeus advances trustworthy LLM-based vulnerability detection by addressing the challenge of implicit security invariants in logic bugs through structured, context-aware reasoning at repository scale.

signals.text: Antaeus detects 15 confirmed logic vulnerabilities across 28 repositories, outperforming function-level and agentic baselines such as Opus 4.7 and 4.8, which analyze fewer functions and yield more false positives.

The method prioritizes functions using lightweight repository-wide security signals to reduce LLM calls and cost, then grounds reasoning in local code plus repository-level context including security resources and trust boundaries.

Comparative validation prunes candidate findings that reflect project-wide norms rather than distinctive violations, improving precision by filtering out false positives caused by common repository conventions.

deep_dive.overview: Logic vulnerabilities differ from memory-safety bugs as they require inferring implicit, application-specific security invariants often distributed across large codebases. Existing LLM-based vulnerability detectors struggle because isolated function-level analysis lacks sufficient context, while exhaustive repository exploration is costly and unfocused. Antaeus addresses this by first prioritizing functions using lightweight heuristics to focus analysis on relevant code regions. It then grounds LLM reasoning in a combined local and repository-level context that includes application functionality, security resources, and trust boundaries, enabling the model to reason about function execution within the broader application. Antaeus identifies security-sensitive sinks, derives safety conditions for safe execution, and checks their local satisfaction. Candidate findings undergo comparative validation to prune false positives reflecting project-wide norms. Evaluated on 28 repositories with confirmed logic vulnerabilities, Antaeus detects and explains 15 vulnerabilities, outperforming function-level and agentic baselines such as Opus 4.7 and 4.8, while maintaining comparable token usage and cost. This demonstrates that structured, context-grounded LLM reasoning at repository scale can effectively detect complex logic vulnerabilities.

methodology.title: Function Prioritization
methodology.detail: Antaeus applies lightweight heuristics to rank functions across the repository using security signals, reducing the number of functions passed to costly LLM analysis and thus lowering computational cost and triage effort.

methodology.title: Context-Grounded Reasoning
methodology.detail: For each prioritized function, Antaeus constructs an input combining local code context with repository-level evidence such as application functionality, security resources, and trust boundaries, enabling the LLM to reason about the function within its broader application context.

methodology.title: Safety Condition Derivation and Checking
methodology.detail: Antaeus identifies security-sensitive sinks in the code, derives the safety conditions required for their safe execution, and uses the LLM to check whether these conditions are locally satisfied within the function.

methodology.title: Comparative Validation
methodology.detail: Candidate vulnerability findings are validated by comparing them against project-wide norms to prune those that reflect common repository conventions rather than distinctive violations, reducing false positives.

methodology.title: Structured Reporting
methodology.detail: Antaeus outputs detailed reports including the identified sinks, violated safety conditions, and supporting evidence, making findings actionable and traceable for security analysts.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide formal equations or causal models but explains that grounding LLM reasoning in repository-level context improves detection by enabling inference of implicit security invariants distributed across code.

experiments.title: Dataset and Evaluation
experiments.detail: Antaeus is evaluated on 28 real-world repositories from the ReposVul dataset, containing 12 CWE-200 and 16 CWE-284 logic vulnerabilities, with ground truth from CVE records and patch commits.

experiments.title: Model Configurations
experiments.detail: Experiments use two frontier LLMs: Claude Opus 4.7 (AntaeusO4.7) and GPT-5.4 (AntaeusG5.4), with additional recall reported for Opus 4.8, all accessed via APIs without local compute.

experiments.title: Baselines and Metrics
experiments.detail: Antaeus is compared against function-level LLM analysis and agentic baselines (Opus 4.7 and 4.8 agentic models), measuring true positives and false positives, with true positives requiring correct sink and safety condition explanations.

experiments.title: Prioritization Impact
experiments.detail: Function prioritization reduces the number of functions analyzed by over 30×, focusing LLM calls on relevant code and reducing cost without sacrificing recall.

findings.title: Superior Detection Performance
findings.detail: Antaeus detects 15 confirmed logic vulnerabilities, outperforming agentic baselines that analyze fewer functions and produce more false positives, e.g., Opus 4.7 agentic analyzes 1,379 functions versus Antaeus’s 4,859.

findings.title: Cost Efficiency
findings.detail: Despite analyzing more functions, Antaeus maintains comparable token usage and cost to baselines by prioritizing functions and grounding reasoning, avoiding exhaustive repository exploration.

findings.title: False Positive Reduction
findings.detail: Comparative validation effectively prunes false positives caused by project-wide norms, improving precision over agentic baselines that increase false positives when supplied with Antaeus’s prioritized function sets.

findings.title: Context Quality Over Quantity
findings.detail: Providing the LLM with structured, repository-level context rather than isolated snippets or exhaustive code enables better inference of implicit security invariants critical for logic vulnerability detection.

contributions: A novel framework, Antaeus, for detecting logic vulnerabilities by grounding LLM reasoning in repository-level context.
A function prioritization technique that reduces analysis cost by focusing LLM calls on relevant code regions.
A comparative validation step that prunes false positives reflecting project-wide norms.
An evaluation on 28 real-world repositories demonstrating superior detection and explanation of logic vulnerabilities compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
limitations: Limited quantitative analysis of false positive rates and scalability beyond the 28 evaluated repositories.
Dependence on heuristic prioritization and vulnerability class-specific sink and safety condition definitions.
No formal mechanistic model or theoretical guarantees provided for the reasoning approach.
Evaluation restricted to C and C++ repositories with logic vulnerabilities from ReposVul dataset.
open_questions: How well does Antaeus generalize to other programming languages and vulnerability classes beyond CWE-200 and CWE-284?
Can the function prioritization heuristics be further optimized or learned to improve recall and precision?
How can the comparative validation step be automated or enhanced to reduce manual tuning?
What are the trade-offs between context size, LLM cost, and detection accuracy in large-scale repositories?

papers.title: Adversarial Pragmatics for AI Safety Evaluation: A Benchmark for Instruction Conflict, Embedded Commands, and Policy Ambiguity
papers.abstract: Safety evaluations for language models increasingly depend on judgments about ambiguous natural-language behaviour: whether a model has followed an instruction, refused appropriately, complied with a policy, resisted an embedded command, or misreported progress in an agentic task. Existing benchmarks often compress these distinctions into pass/fail labels, obscuring whether failures arise from capability limits, policy ambiguity, instruction conflict, scaffold failure, or unstable evaluator judgments. This paper introduces adversarial pragmatics as a benchmark and annotation protocol for evaluating model behaviour under instruction conflict, embedded commands, quotation, scope ambiguity, deixis, indirect speech acts, and multi-turn agent transcripts. The contribution is empirical and methodological: a linguistically controlled taxonomy, an 18-item seed benchmark with validator-enforced metadata, a 54-row local seed pilot, an expert-evaluation protocol distinguishing task success, policy compliance, safety risk, refusal outcome, and evaluator confidence, and metrics for judge validity, diagnostic ambiguity, and taxonomy drift. The framework turns linguistic judgment methodology into a practical tool for validating safety evals, LLM judges, gold-set construction, prompt-injection tests, and safety documentation.
papers.comment: 15-page main paper plus 9-page supplement; 6 figures and 8 tables total; code and data artifact available at the linked repository

summary.takeaway: Adversarial pragmatics provides a linguistically controlled benchmark and annotation protocol to evaluate nuanced safety-relevant behaviors of language models under instruction conflict, embedded commands, and policy ambiguity.
summary.problem: Existing safety benchmarks reduce complex language-model behaviors to pass/fail labels, obscuring failure causes like policy ambiguity, instruction conflict, or evaluator instability.
summary.method: The paper introduces an 18-item seed benchmark with a taxonomy, expert evaluation protocol, validator-enforced metadata, and metrics for judge validity, diagnostic ambiguity, and taxonomy drift.
summary.evidence: A local pilot with three models and expert adjudication showed varied task success and policy compliance rates, revealing stable and unstable linguistic phenomena affecting safety evaluation.
summary.limitations: The pilot uses a small seed set, local models, toy payloads, and a single adjudicator, limiting psychometric validation and frontier-model safety claims.
summary.why_for_you: This work offers a rigorous, linguistically grounded framework to audit and improve LLM safety evaluations by distinguishing subtle pragmatic failures from capability or policy issues.

signals.text: The benchmark distinguishes nuanced refusal outcomes including over-refusal, under-refusal, safe redirection, and incapability masquerading as refusal, enabling fine-grained safety risk assessment beyond binary pass/fail.

The expert-evaluation protocol collects criterion-specific labels for task success, policy compliance, safety risk, refusal outcome, and evaluator confidence, followed by adjudication classifying disagreement sources like annotation error or policy-boundary ambiguity.

Pilot results show that some linguistic contrasts (e.g., embedded-command source, mention/use, scope-negation) yield stable model performance, while others (e.g., deictic-reference, agent transcript, policy boundary) produce zero strict pair passes, indicating diagnostic ambiguity.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of evaluating language models' safety-relevant behaviors that hinge on interpreting ambiguous natural language instructions, policies, and embedded commands. Traditional benchmarks collapse these complex phenomena into pass/fail labels, losing critical information about failure causes. The authors propose adversarial pragmatics as a framework that uses a linguistically controlled taxonomy and a seed benchmark of 18 items organized in minimal pairs to isolate phenomena like instruction conflict, quotation, scope ambiguity, and indirect speech acts. An expert evaluation protocol collects detailed labels on task success, policy compliance, refusal types, and evaluator confidence, with adjudication to diagnose disagreement sources. A local pilot with three models demonstrates the framework's ability to reveal stable and unstable linguistic contrasts affecting safety evaluation. Metrics for judge validity, taxonomy drift, and diagnostic ambiguity enable rigorous auditing of safety claims. The approach transforms linguistic judgment methodology into a practical tool for validating safety evaluations, LLM judges, prompt-injection tests, and safety documentation, thus advancing trustworthy LLM research.

methodology.title: Linguistically Controlled Taxonomy
methodology.detail: Develops a taxonomy capturing distinctions such as instruction conflict, embedded commands, quotation, scope ambiguity, deixis, and indirect speech acts to structure evaluation targets and interpret model behavior under adversarial pragmatics.

methodology.title: Seed Benchmark Construction
methodology.detail: Creates an 18-item seed benchmark organized into nine minimal pairs, each controlling a specific linguistic contrast relevant to safety evaluation, with validator-enforced metadata ensuring item integrity and reproducibility.

methodology.title: Expert-Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: Collects multi-dimensional labels per item including task success, policy compliance, refusal outcome, safety risk, and evaluator confidence, enabling nuanced assessment beyond binary outcomes; followed by adjudication to classify disagreement sources.

methodology.title: Metrics for Judge Validity and Taxonomy Drift
methodology.detail: Introduces metrics to measure judge agreement, label stability under paraphrase and wrapper changes (taxonomy drift), and persistent disagreement (diagnostic ambiguity), supporting robust and auditable safety claims.

methodology.title: Local Pilot Evaluation
methodology.detail: Runs the seed benchmark on three local models with expert adjudication, analyzing task and policy labels, strict pair passes, and disagreement patterns to validate the measurement pipeline and identify stable versus ambiguous phenomena.

mechanism.title: Adversarial Pragmatics Mechanism
mechanism.detail: No explicit formal mechanism or equations are provided; the approach relies on linguistic theory to interpret how language-mediated control failures arise from ambiguous instruction status, source authority, quotation, scope, reference, speech-act force, or policy category.

experiments.title: Local Seed Pilot
experiments.detail: Evaluated 18 seed items in nine minimal pairs across three local models (gemma3:12b, glm-4.7-flash:q4_K_M, qwen3:8b) with expert adjudication labeling task success, policy compliance, refusal outcomes, and confidence; analyzed strict pair passes and disagreement sources.

experiments.title: Adjudication Protocol
experiments.detail: Two-stage adjudication where evaluators first provide criterion-specific labels and confidence without forced consensus, then an adjudicator classifies disagreement sources such as annotation error, missing context, or policy-boundary ambiguity.

experiments.title: Judge Validation
experiments.detail: Comparison of expert labels with LLM-judge annotations showed LLM judges useful as triage tools but not substitutes for expert adjudication, highlighting the need for judge-prompt sensitivity analysis and multiple judge prompts.

findings.title: Task and Policy Label Outcomes
findings.detail: Out of 54 item-model rows, 36 outputs were full task successes, 11 partial successes, and 7 failures; policy compliance was higher with 46 compliant, 7 noncompliant, and 1 ambiguous, indicating policy compliance does not guarantee task success.

findings.title: Phenomenon Stability
findings.detail: Three minimal pairs (embedded-command source, mention/use, scope-negation) were stable across all models, while others (deictic-reference, agent transcript, policy boundary) had zero strict pair passes, revealing linguistic contrasts that challenge model safety.

findings.title: Disagreement as Diagnostic Signal
findings.detail: Persistent evaluator disagreement often indicated genuine ambiguity or underspecified policy boundaries rather than annotation error, supporting the use of disagreement classification to refine taxonomy and evaluation protocols.

findings.title: LLM Judge Limitations
findings.detail: LLM judges underweighted ambiguity and sometimes penalized correct summaries, demonstrating that LLM-based evaluation requires careful validation and cannot replace expert adjudication.

contributions: Introduces adversarial pragmatics as a novel framework for safety evaluation focusing on linguistic control phenomena.
Develops a linguistically controlled taxonomy and an 18-item seed benchmark with validator-enforced metadata.
Proposes an expert-evaluation protocol capturing multi-dimensional labels and adjudication to diagnose disagreement sources.
Defines metrics for judge validity, taxonomy drift, and diagnostic ambiguity to support robust safety claims.
Demonstrates feasibility and diagnostic value through a local pilot with three models and expert adjudication.
limitations: The pilot uses a small, hand-authored seed set of 18 items, limiting generalizability and psychometric validation.
Only three local models with toy payloads were evaluated, so results do not establish frontier-model safety differences.
A single expert adjudicator was used, restricting assessment of adjudication reliability and population-level evaluator behavior.
LLM-judge validation remains preliminary and requires further experiments with multiple prompts and adjudicators.
open_questions: How does the benchmark scale and perform with a larger, more diverse item set and frontier models?
What is the reliability and validity of multi-adjudicator protocols across different evaluator populations?
How can LLM judges be reliably calibrated and validated to complement or partially automate expert adjudication?
Which linguistic phenomena most critically impact safety evaluation stability and how can taxonomy drift be minimized?

papers.title: Truth or Sophistry? LoFa: A Benchmark for LLM Robustness Against Logical Fallacies
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong semantic capabilities, yet their resilience to manipulative linguistic patterns such as logical fallacies remains underexplored. Prior work has primarily examined whether LLMs can identify or classify fallacies, leaving their robustness against fallacious persuasion insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we introduce LoFa (Logical Fallacy), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM robustness against fallacies. LoFa is constructed through a multi-agent pipeline that pairs factual questions with fallacious arguments, and is accompanied by a multi-round debate framework for assessing model resilience under sustained adversarial persuasion. To disentangle fallacy robustness from a model's inherent knowledge limitations, we further propose Logical Fallacy Resistance at k (LFR@k), a metric that quantifies resistance to fallacious attacks. Experiments show that LLMs exhibit varying levels of robustness across different fallacy types, revealing distinct vulnerability profiles among models.
papers.comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Main. 33 pages (9 pages main text)

summary.takeaway: LoFa benchmark reveals that LLMs exhibit varied robustness to different logical fallacies, with notable vulnerabilities to distraction/distortion fallacies and a surprising deference to authority.
summary.problem: Existing research focuses on LLMs' ability to identify fallacies but neglects their robustness against fallacious persuasive attacks.
summary.method: LoFa constructs a dataset pairing factual questions with fallacious arguments and employs a multi-round debate framework alongside the LFR@k metric to quantify LLM resistance to fallacies.
summary.evidence: Experiments show LLMs like Llama-3.1 and GPT-4 have distinct vulnerability profiles, with LFR@3 scores as low as 29.4% for Equivocation and 39.2% for Appeal to Authority fallacies.
summary.limitations: LoFa's limited scale (~2000 items) and evaluation on a narrow set of dense, decoder-only LLM architectures constrain generalizability.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding LLM susceptibility to logical fallacies is critical for developing trustworthy models resilient to manipulative linguistic attacks.

signals.text: LLMs show higher resistance to fallacies involving flawed reasoning (e.g., Hasty Generalization) but are more vulnerable to distraction/distortion fallacies like Equivocation and Straw Man, with Llama-3.1-405B scoring only 29.4% LFR@3 on Equivocation.

The LoFa benchmark uses a multi-agent pipeline to pair factual questions from Wikipedia-derived datasets with fallacious arguments, evaluated via a multi-round debate framework and the novel LFR@k metric to isolate fallacy resistance from knowledge limitations.

GPT-4 exhibits a cognitive deference to fabricated authoritative cues in the Appeal to Authority fallacy, resulting in a low LFR@3 score of 39.2%, likely due to RLHF training bias favoring context adherence over factual verification.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the underexplored problem of LLM robustness against logical fallacies used as manipulative persuasive attacks. Unlike prior work focusing on fallacy identification, the authors introduce LoFa, a benchmark that rigorously evaluates LLMs' passive resilience by pairing objective factual questions with fallacious arguments crafted via a multi-agent pipeline. The evaluation employs a multi-round debate framework and a novel metric, LFR@k, to quantify resistance while disentangling it from inherent knowledge gaps. Experiments across multiple LLMs, including open-source Llama-3.1 variants and closed-source GPT models, reveal distinct vulnerability profiles. Models generally resist flawed reasoning fallacies but are susceptible to distraction/distortion fallacies, with Llama models particularly vulnerable. Notably, GPT models show a pronounced deference to authority, undermining resistance to the Appeal to Authority fallacy. Attempts to mitigate this via chain-of-thought prompting yield mixed results. The benchmark's modest scale and limited model diversity constrain generalizability, but the findings highlight critical weaknesses in LLM reasoning robustness and suggest directions for future research to enhance trustworthy AI.

methodology.title: LoFa Dataset Construction
methodology.detail: LoFa is constructed by pairing factual questions from Wikipedia-derived datasets (Natural Questions, TruthfulQA, BoolQ) with fallacious arguments generated via a multi-agent pipeline. The dataset covers 10 logical fallacies categorized into Distraction/Distortion and Flaws in Reasoning/Evidence, ensuring objective ground truth for evaluation.

methodology.title: Multi-Round Debate Framework
methodology.detail: The evaluation framework simulates sustained adversarial persuasion by engaging LLMs in multi-turn debates where fallacious arguments challenge the model's initial correct answers, measuring the model's ability to maintain factual correctness under pressure.

methodology.title: Logical Fallacy Resistance Metric (LFR@k)
methodology.detail: LFR@k quantifies the model's resistance to fallacious attacks by measuring the proportion of rounds in which the model maintains correct answers despite fallacious persuasion, effectively separating robustness from knowledge limitations.

methodology.title: Model Selection and Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: The study evaluates multiple LLMs including Llama-3.1 (8B, 70B, 405B), DeepSeek-V3 (~671B), GPT-3.5 Turbo (~175B), and GPT-4 (~1760B). Closed-source models were accessed via API calls. Performance is averaged over three runs and analyzed per fallacy type.

mechanism.title: Cognitive Deference to Authority
mechanism.detail: GPT models' susceptibility to the Appeal to Authority fallacy is hypothesized to stem from RLHF training, which rewards context adherence and may bias models to accept authoritative cues without verification, overriding internal factual knowledge.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanistic Equations
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide formal mechanistic equations or causal models but discusses the cognitive and training-induced biases influencing LLM fallacy resilience.

experiments.title: Fallacy Resistance Evaluation on NQ1 Dataset
experiments.detail: Models were tested on a subset of the Natural Questions dataset (NQ1) with 488 samples, paired with fallacious arguments representing 10 fallacy types. Resistance was measured using LFR@3 scores across multiple rounds of debate.

experiments.title: Model Scale Impact Analysis
experiments.detail: Within the Llama-3.1 family, increasing model size from 8B to 405B parameters consistently improved average LFR@3 scores from 59.75% to 77.17%, demonstrating a positive scaling effect on fallacy resistance.

experiments.title: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting Defense
experiments.detail: Applying CoT prompting to GPT-4 improved average LFR@3 scores by 7-13% for most fallacies but decreased resistance by 1.87% for the Appeal to Authority, indicating CoT's limited efficacy against authority-based fallacies.

experiments.title: Active Argument Generation vs. Passive Resilience
experiments.detail: An additional experiment compared DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-4 on their ability to generate persuasive arguments and resist fallacious persuasion, exploring the relationship between active generation capabilities and passive robustness.

findings.title: Vulnerability to Distraction/Distortion Fallacies
findings.detail: LLMs are more susceptible to distraction/distortion fallacies such as Equivocation and Straw Man, with Llama-3.1-405B scoring only 29.4% and 57.0% LFR@3 respectively, indicating these fallacies effectively exploit semantic shortcuts.

findings.title: Robustness to Flaws in Reasoning/Evidence Fallacies
findings.detail: Models generally show higher resistance to fallacies involving flawed reasoning like Hasty Generalization and Circular Reasoning, suggesting better handling of logical inconsistencies than semantic distractions.

findings.title: Scaling Improves Fallacy Resistance
findings.detail: Within the Llama-3.1 series, larger models consistently achieve higher LFR@3 scores, with the 405B parameter model reaching 77.17%, confirming that increased scale enhances robustness.

findings.title: GPT Models’ Deference to Authority
findings.detail: GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-4 exhibit pronounced vulnerability to the Appeal to Authority fallacy, with LFR@3 scores of 22.54% and 39.20% respectively, attributed to cognitive deference induced by RLHF.

findings.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Effects
findings.detail: CoT prompting improves GPT-4’s resistance to most fallacies by 7-13% but paradoxically reduces resistance to the Appeal to Authority fallacy by 1.87%, highlighting nuanced effects of reasoning enhancements.

contributions: Introduction of LoFa, a novel benchmark pairing factual questions with fallacious arguments to evaluate LLM robustness against logical fallacies.
Development of a multi-round debate framework simulating sustained adversarial persuasion for rigorous robustness assessment.
Proposal of the LFR@k metric to quantify fallacy resistance while controlling for knowledge limitations.
Comprehensive evaluation of multiple LLMs revealing distinct vulnerability profiles and the impact of model scale.
Identification of GPT models’ cognitive deference to authority as a critical vulnerability linked to RLHF training.
limitations: LoFa benchmark size is limited (~2000 items), potentially restricting statistical generalizability across domains and linguistic styles.
Evaluation focuses on a narrow set of dense, decoder-only LLM architectures, leaving uncertainty about generalization to other model types like Mixture-of-Experts.
The study does not explore mechanistic causal models or formal theoretical explanations for observed vulnerabilities.
Mitigation strategies such as CoT prompting show limited efficacy, especially against authority-based fallacies, indicating a need for more robust defenses.
open_questions: How can LLM training paradigms be adapted to reduce cognitive deference to fabricated authoritative cues without sacrificing context adherence?
What architectural or training modifications can enhance LLM robustness specifically against distraction/distortion fallacies?
Can larger and more diverse datasets improve the statistical reliability and domain generalization of fallacy resistance benchmarks?
What is the relationship between a model’s active argument generation quality and its passive resilience to fallacious persuasion?

papers.title: HARC: Coupling Harmfulness and Refusal Directions for Robust Safety Alignment
papers.abstract: Understanding how aligned LLMs internally represent safety is critical for diagnosing alignment vulnerabilities, as it explains why jailbreaks succeed and informs the design of robust alignment strategies. Prior work shows that aligned LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separable directions in the residual stream at prompt-side token positions. We show that jailbreaks succeed at prompt encoding by suppressing either the refusal or harmfulness direction before any token is generated, with distinct attack classes occupying separable regions of the harmfulness-refusal plane. Extending the analysis to response-token positions, we find that the model recognizes harmful content while it is generating that content, even when it failed to recognize the input as harmful at the prompt side. Motivated by our findings, we introduce HARC (Harmfulness-And-Refusal Coupling), a fine-tuning method that pairs the two directions across both prompt and response positions. Since the intervention is confined to the harmfulness-refusal subspace, it leaves the rest of the residual stream intact and does not degrade general capability or inflate over-refusal. Across extensive experiments, HARC achieves the strongest robustness-capability-usability trade-off among six baselines spanning the major training-time and inference-time safety methods. The harmfulness and refusal directions at prompt and response positions transfer across the five model families and two scales we tested without architecture-specific tuning.

summary.takeaway: HARC fine-tuning couples harmfulness and refusal directions at both prompt and response positions, achieving superior robustness and usability without degrading general capability.
summary.problem: Aligned LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separable directions, allowing jailbreak attacks to suppress refusal or harmfulness signals and bypass safety alignment.
summary.method: HARC fine-tunes models by coupling harmfulness and refusal directions in the residual stream subspace at prompt and response tokens, enforcing refusal activation whenever harmfulness is detected.
summary.evidence: Experiments on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B across four jailbreak attacks, over-refusal benchmarks, and capability tests show HARC achieves the best robustness-capability-usability trade-off among six baselines.
summary.limitations: CodeAttack jailbreaks remain partially resistant as their residual activations are orthogonal to harmfulness and refusal directions, limiting coupling loss gradients.
summary.why_for_you: HARC provides an interpretable, efficient adversarial training approach that improves trustworthy LLM safety alignment by leveraging internal harmfulness-refusal representations without sacrificing model utility.

signals.text: Jailbreak attacks like DAN and PAIR exploit the dissociation between harmfulness (vharm) and refusal (vref) directions by suppressing one direction at prompt encoding, enabling harmful responses despite refusal signals.

HARC fine-tuning couples vharm and vref directions at layers L25–L28 (Llama) and L21–L24 (Qwen) using LoRA adapters, reshaping residual activations to propagate refusal whenever harmfulness is detected.

Coupling fine-tuning collapses dissociated regions exploited by jailbreaks, compressing harmful, DAN, and PAIR clusters into a single ridge along the diagonal in the harmfulness-refusal plane, reducing attack success rates.

deep_dive.overview: This work investigates how aligned large language models internally represent safety via harmfulness and refusal directions in the residual stream. Prior work identified these as separable at prompt tokens, but this paper extends analysis to response tokens, revealing that models recognize harmful content during generation even if prompt-side recognition fails. Jailbreak attacks exploit this dissociation by suppressing refusal or harmfulness directions, enabling harmful outputs. Motivated by this, the authors propose HARC, a fine-tuning method that couples harmfulness and refusal directions at both prompt and response positions, enforcing refusal activation whenever harmfulness is detected. This coupling is confined to a two-dimensional subspace, preserving general capabilities and avoiding over-refusal. Extensive experiments on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B models across multiple jailbreak attacks, over-refusal, and capability benchmarks demonstrate that HARC achieves the strongest robustness-capability-usability trade-off compared to six baselines. The harmfulness-refusal structure and HARC’s effectiveness transfer across five model families and two scales without architecture-specific tuning, highlighting a general property of aligned LLMs and a promising alignment strategy.

methodology.title: Direction Extraction
methodology.detail: Harmfulness (vharm) and refusal (vref) directions are extracted from residual stream activations at both prompt-side and response-side token positions, identifying subspaces encoding safety concepts.

methodology.title: Coupling Fine-Tuning
methodology.detail: HARC fine-tunes models by applying a coupling loss that increases cosine similarity between vharm and vref directions within selected layers (L25–L28 for Llama, L21–L24 for Qwen), using LoRA adapters on attention and MLP projections, with directions recomputed every 200 steps.

methodology.title: Dual-Position Objective
methodology.detail: The coupling loss is applied simultaneously at prompt and response token positions to ensure refusal activation propagates regardless of where harmful intent is first detected, reducing over-refusal and preserving helpfulness.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: Attack success rate (ASR) is measured using an LLM judge (GPT-4o) with the HexPHI scoring template on JailbreakBench attacks; over-refusal is evaluated on XSTest and CoCoNot; general capability is assessed on MMLU, GSM8K, IFEval, HumanEval, and MT-Bench.

mechanism.title: Harmfulness-Refusal Direction Coupling
mechanism.detail: The model’s residual stream contains distinct vharm and vref directions that are nearly orthogonal at late layers, allowing inputs to activate harmfulness without refusal. HARC reshapes this subspace by increasing cosine similarity between vharm and vref, causing refusal activation to reliably follow harmfulness detection, thus blocking jailbreaks that suppress refusal.

experiments.title: Model Fine-Tuning and Baselines
experiments.detail: Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B models are fine-tuned with HARC using LoRA adapters; six baselines include supervised fine-tuning (SFT), DPO, Circuit Breakers, RepBend, and CAST, covering major training-time and inference-time safety methods.

experiments.title: Jailbreak Attack Evaluation
experiments.detail: Four jailbreak attacks (DAN, PAIR, CodeAttack, DeepInception) are evaluated on JailbreakBench using GPT-4o judge to compute attack success rates, assessing robustness improvements from HARC and baselines.

experiments.title: Over-Refusal and Capability Benchmarks
experiments.detail: Over-refusal is measured on XSTest and CoCoNot datasets; general capability is evaluated on MMLU, GSM8K, IFEval, HumanEval, and MT-Bench to verify that HARC preserves usability and helpfulness.

findings.title: Jailbreaks Exploit Direction Dissociation
findings.detail: DAN and PAIR attacks suppress refusal or harmfulness directions at prompt encoding, enabling harmful responses; CodeAttack suppresses both, remaining orthogonal to these directions.

findings.title: Response-Side Recognition of Harmfulness
findings.detail: Models recognize harmful content during generation even when prompt-side harmfulness detection fails, indicating a four-direction structure at response tokens.

findings.title: HARC Collapses Dissociated Regions
findings.detail: Coupling fine-tuning compresses harmful, DAN, and PAIR clusters into a single ridge along the diagonal in the harmfulness-refusal plane, reducing attack success rates and improving robustness.

findings.title: Preservation of Capability and Over-Refusal
findings.detail: HARC confines intervention to the harmfulness-refusal subspace, avoiding degradation of general capabilities and preventing inflation of over-refusal rates, unlike other baselines.

findings.title: CodeAttack Remains Partially Resistant
findings.detail: CodeAttack residuals are nearly orthogonal to vharm and vref, limiting gradient signals for coupling loss and making it the hardest attack to fully mitigate.

contributions: Identification of a four-direction harmfulness-refusal structure at prompt and response token positions in aligned LLMs.
Demonstration that jailbreak attacks exploit dissociation between harmfulness and refusal directions to bypass safety.
Introduction of HARC, a fine-tuning method coupling harmfulness and refusal directions to enforce refusal activation upon harmfulness detection.
Extensive evaluation showing HARC’s superior robustness-capability-usability trade-off across multiple models, attacks, and benchmarks.
Evidence that harmfulness and refusal directions and HARC’s effectiveness generalize across model families and scales without architecture-specific tuning.
limitations: CodeAttack jailbreaks remain partially resistant due to orthogonality to harmfulness and refusal directions, limiting coupling loss effectiveness.
The approach relies on accurate extraction of harmfulness and refusal directions, which may vary with model architecture or training data.
No explicit mechanism or theoretical proof is provided for why coupling these directions improves refusal propagation beyond empirical evidence.
Evaluation is limited to instruction-tuned models and specific jailbreak attacks; broader generalization to other attack types or model classes is untested.
open_questions: Can HARC be extended or adapted to mitigate jailbreaks like CodeAttack that evade harmfulness-refusal coupling?
How stable and consistent are harmfulness and refusal directions across diverse model architectures and training regimes?
What are the theoretical underpinnings explaining why coupling harmfulness and refusal directions improves alignment robustness?
Can the harmfulness-refusal coupling approach be integrated with other alignment strategies to further reduce the alignment tax?

papers.title: Ghost in the Kernel: In-Context Learning with Efficient Transformers via Domain Generalization
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large models have demonstrated remarkable generalization abilities across different tasks by leveraging a context-aware attention module for in-context learning. With richer context, transformers adapt more effectively to the current use case without any parameter updates. However, the quadratic computational and memory complexity with respect to context length significantly slows data processing in softmax transformers. Linear transformers were proposed to address this issue by reducing the complexity to linear dependence on context length, but the design and understanding of the feature mapping in linear attention, from a theoretical viewpoint, remain unclear. In this paper, we investigate the approximation and generalization abilities of linear transformers under a two-staged sampling process from domain generalization. We show that linear transformers perform in-context learning as learning a mapping from context distributions to response functions. A dimension-independent convergence rate is obtained for our generalization analysis, which also exhibits the tradeoff between the regularities of data distributions and latent features. Guided by our theoretical framework, we propose a new perspective on activation and loss design for linearizing pretrained softmax large language models.

summary.takeaway: Linear transformers enhance in-context learning by leveraging domain generalization principles.
summary.problem: Quadratic complexity in softmax transformers limits their efficiency in processing long contexts.
summary.method: The paper proposes a two-staged sampling process to analyze linear transformers' approximation and generalization abilities.
summary.evidence: A dimension-independent convergence rate is established, demonstrating the tradeoff between data distribution regularities and latent features.
summary.limitations: The theoretical understanding of linear attention mechanisms remains limited despite empirical successes.
summary.why_for_you: This research provides insights into improving LLM efficiency and generalization, relevant for statistical theory and data selection.

signals.text: The paper establishes that linear transformers perform in-context learning as a mapping from context distributions to response functions, enhancing their generalization capabilities.
A two-staged sampling process is introduced to analyze linear transformers, connecting in-context learning with domain generalization frameworks.
The authors demonstrate a dimension-independent convergence rate in their generalization analysis, revealing a tradeoff between data distribution regularities and latent feature representation.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the inefficiencies of softmax transformers in long-context scenarios due to their quadratic computational complexity. By investigating linear transformers through a two-staged sampling process, the authors connect in-context learning with domain generalization, revealing that linear transformers can effectively generalize across tasks without parameter updates. The strongest evidence presented is a dimension-independent convergence rate, which highlights the tradeoff between the regularities of data distributions and latent features, thus providing a theoretical foundation for improving transformer architectures in practical applications.

methodology.title: Two-Staged Sampling Process
